newsitem.title: USA: SOYMEAL--U.S. supplies seen tight until January.
newsitem.headline: SOYMEAL--U.S. supplies seen tight until January.

text.p: Tight U.S. soymeal supplies this fall have frustrated bargain hunters who have held off purchases hoping cash basis levels would fall, cash soymeal dealers said.
Instead basis levels have risen, supported by a late U.S. soybean harvest and an active soymeal export program. As a result, very little soymeal is available for November or December needs.
Even with processing plants running at high levels, soymeal demand is keeping pace with production, sources said.
The National Oilseed Processing Association reported 29.84 million bushels of soybeans were crushed the week ended October 30, which many dealers said was a record-large amount.
One soymeal dealer said basis levels have gone from $3 per ton under the spot Chicago Board of Trade futures in September to $15 over now, basis central Illinois.
"As long as the export market stays good, the domestic market will stay tight," said an Illinois dealer.
Some analysts said soymeal supply and price relief may occur by late December, while others said it could be March, 1997 when the South American soybean crop is harvested.
A key reason for the current tightness was sales in October to China, which caught the domestic market by surprise.
"You put 35 percent of your production down the river two weeks ago," said Roy Huckabay, analyst with LIT America, referring to recent export sales.
Soymeal sales are running ahead of a year ago, with the U.S. Agriculture Department (USDA) reporting sales through October 24 at 1.93 million tonnes versus 996,000 a year ago.
"It is pretty unusual for exports to be this strong," said Dale Gustafson, analyst with Smith Barney.

One reason for the export surge is, South America is running out, leaving the United States the primary supplier of soymeal, Gustafson said. As a result, he expects the U.S. to export 6.2 million tonnes this year versus the latest USDA estimate of 5.44 million.
Although basis levels have risen, cash prices for soymeal have dropped about $40 per short ton the past month, said cash dealers, because of the six-week decline in CBOT soymeal futures.

Gustafson said the drop in CBOT soymeal futures was keyed to recent increases in estimates for the U.S. crop rather than to soymeal demand. In October, USDA pegged the soybean crop at 2.346 billion bushels, up from the 2.270 million forecast in September.
"Not only did the crop (expectations) get bigger, but they (traders) think it may get bigger," he said.
